concept.name: Guidance
concept.definition: A public company's own forecast of its future performance - typically revenue and EPS for the coming quarter or year - issued voluntarily alongside earnings reports and discussed on analyst calls. It shapes the consensus against which actual results are later judged.
concept.intuition: Guidance is management's answer to 'what should we expect?' - and it often matters more to the stock than the quarter just reported.
concept.mechanics: Companies typically release guidance with quarterly results and may update it mid-quarter via pre-announcements. Under Regulation FD it must be shared with all investors simultaneously, and the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act's safe harbor shields good-faith forward-looking statements that turn out wrong.
concept.failure_modes: Management incentives skew it - conservative 'sandbagging' to manufacture beats or promotional optimism - and companies are under no obligation to update guidance even when events make it stale.
concept.misconceptions: Guidance is not required disclosure and not a promise: it is an estimate protected by safe-harbor provisions, and critics such as Warren Buffett argue quarterly guidance pushes managers toward short-termism.
concept.example: A company guiding to $4.00-4.20 of EPS that reports $4.05 is treated as 'in line'; the identical $4.05 against $4.50 guidance counts as a miss despite equal profits.
